title: What's this? The wardrobe is a "he"
goal: Ask about and name the things around you, then accept the first big fact of Russian: every noun has a gender, including tables, windows and milk.
bekal: ask "what is this?" and "who is this?"
name the things in a room
tell a noun's gender from its last letter
use он / она / оно for objects

dialogs.title: Диалог — Seeing the room
dialogs.intro: Ani has just moved into a dormitory. The warden, Ольга Петровна, shows her to her room. Notice that the things in the room are called "he" and "she" — and not always the same one.

lines.speaker: Ольга:
lines.id: Yes, the wardrobe is "he". The bed is "she". The window is "it".
lines.literal: yes, wardrobe — he. and — bed — she. and — window — it.

lines.speaker: Ольга:
lines.id: Don't worry. It's simple: look at the last letter.
lines.literal: not — worry. this — simple: look — at — last — letter.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: And who's this? In the photo.

lines.speaker: Ольга:
lines.id: No! He's everywhere. This is Russia.

notes: **Что это? for things, Кто это? for people.** Just like English "what" and "who", so the split feels natural right away. ⚠️ The trap is the pronunciation: **что** is said *shto*, not *chto*. The ч in this word — and in **конечно** (*ka-NYESH-na*, of course) — is said *sh*. Those are the only two words you need to remember at A1.

**Это means "this/that/it" as a general pointer, and its form never changes.** *Это шкаф*, *Это кровать*, *Это окно* — the same это for all three genders. It only changes when used as an adjective (*этот шкаф* — this wardrobe), which isn't covered in this unit.

**Вот is not the same as Это.** Вот is used while pointing at or handing over something — "here it is", "here you go", "there it is". Это identifies — "this is". *Вот ваша комната* = "here's your room" (opening the door). *Это ваша комната* = "this is your room" (explaining).

**Even objects are "he" or "she".** ⚠️ This is the big surprise for English speakers, whose objects are all "it". In Russian a wardrobe is *он*, a bed is *она*, a window is *оно* — and you have to follow suit to be understood. There is no hidden meaning: nobody thinks a wardrobe is more manly than a bed. It's pure grammar.
**The good news: you can read the gender from the last letter**, and the rule covers more than ninety percent of nouns. The grammar box below contains the whole rule — it really is that short.
**Понятно** (*pa-NYAT-na*) is a word you'll use constantly: "got it", "clear", "I see". The opposite is **Непонятно** — "not clear".

**Он жил — past-tense verbs follow the gender of the subject.** It's not time for the full story yet (Unit 14), but notice it now: if the person who lived there were a woman, the sentence would be *она жи**ла***. The ending **-л** for a man, **-ла** for a woman.

grammars.title: Three noun genders — read from the last letter
body: Look at the **very last** letter of the dictionary form. That's all. You don't need to know what the word means or where it comes from.

head: Ends in
Gender
Pronoun
Examples
rows: a consonant (б, в, г, д, к, м, н, п, р, с, т, ф…)

after: ⚠️ Words ending in **-ь** are the one hole in the system: the last letter tells you nothing, so the gender has to be learned with the word. Luckily there aren't many at A1. In this course such words are always marked **(f)** or **(m)** in the vocabulary tables.
For people, the gender follows the person's sex, and that beats the last letter: **папа** (dad) ends in -а but is still **он**. Same for **мужчина** (man).

Why this matters from day one: everything that comes next — adjectives, possessives, case endings, past tense — depends on the noun's gender. Get the gender wrong here and everything downstream goes wrong too.

blocks.text: The most useful practice for this unit: walk around your own room naming every object with its pronoun. *Стол — он. Дверь — она. Окно — оно.* Five minutes a day for a week, and noun gender stops feeling strange.

blocks.title: Loanwords: a free gift
items: Russian has absorbed thousands of international words, and you already know what many of them mean before learning anything: **телефон**, **компьютер**, **такси**, **банк**, **отель**, **интернет**, **офис**, **кофе**, **аэропорт**, **паспорт**, **музыка**, **студент**.

All you need to practice is reading them in Cyrillic and putting the stress in the right place — often **not** where English puts it. Compare English *TEL-e-phone* with Russian **ti-li-FON**, and *com-PU-ter* with **kam-P'YU-ter**.

⚠️ One trap: **кофе** (coffee) ends in -е, so by the rule it should be neuter — but it's **masculine**, a leftover from its old form кофей. Russians themselves argue about it. Use *он* and you're safe.

exercises.prompt: Write the pronoun: он, она or оно.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: он — она — оно — он — она — оно
Что это? — Это шкаф. — Он большой. — Вот ваша комната. — Он поэт.
Что это? — Это дверь. — Она маленькая. — Кто это? — Это врач. — Вот твоя книга.
